es.summary: Consumo de una dosis excesiva de opioides que produce depresión respiratoria, pérdida de conciencia y riesgo de muerte. Requiere intervención rápida con antagonista opioide y soporte vital.
key_points: Los opioides deprimen el centro respiratorio del bulbo raquídeo.
Miosis, respiración lenta (<8 rpm) y nivel de conciencia disminuido son signos clásicos.
Naloxona (DIC) revierte rápidamente la depresión respiratoria.
El riesgo aumenta con dosis altas, uso concomitante de depresores del SNC y uso no prescrito.
El manejo incluye aseguramiento de la vía aérea y monitorización continua.

pathophysiology: Los opioides se unen a receptores μ en el tronco encefálico, reduciendo la sensibilidad a CO₂.
Disminuye la frecuencia y profundidad respiratoria, provocando hipoventilación.
Hipoventilación lleva a hipercapnia, acidosis respiratoria y disminución de O₂ arterial.
La hipoxia cerebral produce pérdida de conciencia y posible muerte.
risk_factors: Dosis alta o acumulación por insuficiente metabolismo renal/hepático.
Uso simultáneo de benzodiacepinas, alcohol o otros depresores del SNC.
Historia de trastorno por consumo de opioides.
Administración intravenosa de opioides ilícitos (ej. heroína).
diagnostics: Frecuencia respiratoria y saturación de O₂ (SpO₂ < 90%).
Tóxico urinario para opioides si está disponible.
ECG si se sospecha arritmia por hipoxia.
treatment: Administrar naloxona 0.4‑2 mg IV/IM/SC; repetir cada 2‑3 min si persiste depresión.
Asegurar vía aérea: posición lateral de seguridad o intubación si es necesario.
Oxígeno suplementario 2‑4 L/min por cánula nasal o máscara facial.
Monitoreo continuo de signos vitales y nivel de conciencia.
complications: Hipoxia cerebral con daño neurológico permanente.
Lesiones por caídas durante la pérdida de conciencia.
nursing_care: Evaluar frecuencia respiratoria, SpO₂ y nivel de conciencia cada 2‑5 min.
Mantener vía aérea abierta; colocar al paciente en decúbito supino con cabeza ligeramente elevada.
Administrar naloxona según orden y observar respuesta clínica.
Registrar pupilas y cambios en la respiración después de cada dosis.
Preparar equipo de reanimación y notificar al médico inmediatamente.
patient_teaching: Usar opioides solo según prescripción y nunca compartirlos.
Almacenar en un lugar seguro fuera del alcance de niños y personas no autorizadas.
Reconocer signos de sobredosis: respiración lenta, pupilas contraídas, somnolencia.
Llamar al 911 o acudir a urgencias ante sospecha de sobredosis.
Entregar naloxona de rescate a pacientes con alto riesgo y enseñar su uso.

related_to: uso de opioides en dosis altas
outcomes: Integridad de vías respiratorias: sin evidencia de aspiración durante la estancia

interventions.action: Colocar al paciente en posición lateral de seguridad inmediatamente después de la administración de naloxona.
interventions.rationale: Facilita el drenaje de secreciones y reduce el riesgo de aspiración.

interventions.action: Mantener la cabeza del lecho elevada 30‑45° mientras el paciente está consciente.
interventions.rationale: Mejora el flujo aéreo y disminuye la probabilidad de ingreso de contenido gástrico.

interventions.action: Evaluar presencia de vómitos o secreciones orofaríngeas cada 5 minutos.
interventions.rationale: Detecta rápidamente material que pueda ser aspirado.

interventions.action: Administrar oxígeno suplementario y monitorizar SpO₂ continuamente.
interventions.rationale: Compensa la hipoxemia y permite detección precoz de deterioro respiratorio.

interventions.action: Educar al paciente y acompañante sobre signos de aspiración y cuándo buscar ayuda.
interventions.rationale: Promueve la detección temprana y la intervención oportuna.

care_plans.diagnosis: Riesgo de perfusión tisular cerebral ineficaz
outcomes: Perfusión cerebral: mantener presión arterial sistólica ≥ 100 mmHg

interventions.action: Monitorear presión arterial y frecuencia cardíaca cada 5 minutos.
interventions.rationale: Detecta hipotensión que pueda comprometer la perfusión cerebral.

interventions.action: Administrar naloxona según protocolo y observar mejoría de la respiración.
interventions.rationale: Revierte la depresión respiratoria y restaura la oxigenación cerebral.

interventions.action: Proveer oxígeno a 2‑4 L/min y ajustar según SpO₂.
interventions.rationale: Aumenta la fracción inspirada de O₂, mejorando la entrega a los tejidos cerebrales.

interventions.action: Realizar evaluación neurológica (Escala de Glasgow) cada 15 minutos.
interventions.rationale: Permite detectar cambios en el nivel de conciencia que indiquen deterioro cerebral.

interventions.action: Preparar y, si es necesario, iniciar ventilación mecánica invasiva.
interventions.rationale: Garantiza ventilación adecuada cuando la respiración espontánea es insuficiente.

en.summary: Consumption of an excessive dose of opioids that produces respiratory depression, loss of consciousness, and risk of death. Requires rapid intervention with opioid antagonist and life support.
key_points: Opioids depress the respiratory center in the medulla.
Miosis, slow breathing (<8 breaths/min) and decreased level of consciousness are classic signs.
Risk increases with high doses, concomitant use of CNS depressants, and non-prescribed use.
Management includes securing the airway and continuous monitoring.

pathophysiology: Opioids bind to μ receptors in the brainstem, reducing CO₂ sensitivity.
Respiratory rate and depth decrease, causing hypoventilation.
Hypoventilation leads to hypercapnia, respiratory acidosis, and decreased arterial O₂.
Cerebral hypoxia causes loss of consciousness and possible death.
risk_factors: High dose or accumulation due to insufficient renal/hepatic metabolism.
Concurrent use of benzodiazepines, alcohol, or other CNS depressants.
Intravenous administration of illicit opioids (e.g., heroin).
diagnostics: Urine toxicology for opioids if available.
ECG if arrhythmia suspected from hypoxia.
treatment: Administer naloxone 0.4‑2 mg IV/IM/SC; repeat every 2‑3 min if depression persists.
Secure airway: use the recovery position or intubate if necessary.
Supplemental oxygen 2‑4 L/min via nasal cannula or face mask.
Continuous monitoring of vital signs and level of consciousness.
complications: Cerebral hypoxia with permanent neurological damage.
Fall injuries during loss of consciousness.
nursing_care: Assess respiratory rate, SpO₂, and level of consciousness every 2‑5 min.
Keep airway open; place patient supine with head slightly elevated.
Administer naloxone per order and observe clinical response.
Document pupils and respiratory changes after each dose.
Prepare resuscitation equipment and notify the physician immediately.
patient_teaching: Use opioids only as prescribed and never share them.
Store in a secure place out of reach of children and unauthorized persons.
Recognize overdose signs: slow breathing, constricted pupils, drowsiness.
Call 911 or go to the emergency department if overdose is suspected.
Provide rescue naloxone to high-risk patients and teach its use.

outcomes: Airway integrity: no evidence of aspiration during stay

interventions.action: Place the patient in the recovery position immediately after naloxone administration.
interventions.rationale: Facilitates drainage of secretions and reduces aspiration risk.

interventions.action: Keep the head of the bed elevated 30‑45° while the patient is conscious.
interventions.rationale: Improves airflow and decreases the likelihood of gastric content entry.

interventions.action: Assess for vomiting or oropharyngeal secretions every 5 minutes.
interventions.rationale: Rapidly detects material that could be aspirated.

interventions.action: Administer supplemental oxygen and monitor SpO₂ continuously.
interventions.rationale: Compensates for hypoxemia and allows early detection of respiratory deterioration.

interventions.action: Educate the patient and companion about aspiration signs and when to seek help.
interventions.rationale: Promotes early detection and timely intervention.

care_plans.diagnosis: Risk for ineffective cerebral tissue perfusion
outcomes: Cerebral perfusion: maintain systolic blood pressure ≥ 100 mmHg

interventions.action: Monitor blood pressure and heart rate every 5 minutes.
interventions.rationale: Detects hypotension that could compromise cerebral perfusion.

interventions.action: Administer naloxone per protocol and observe respiratory improvement.
interventions.rationale: Reverses respiratory depression and restores cerebral oxygenation.

interventions.action: Provide oxygen at 2‑4 L/min and titrate to SpO₂.
interventions.rationale: Increases inspired oxygen fraction, improving delivery to cerebral tissues.

interventions.action: Perform neurological assessment (Glasgow Scale) every 15 minutes.
interventions.rationale: Allows detection of changes in consciousness indicating cerebral deterioration.

interventions.action: Prepare and, if necessary, initiate invasive mechanical ventilation.
interventions.rationale: Ensures adequate ventilation when spontaneous breathing is insufficient.

key_points.2.quote: While naloxone rapidly reverses the effects of opioids within seconds to minutes, it only lasts approximately 20–30 minutes, which is less than the duration of action of many opioids.

key_points.3.quote: Concomitant use of opioids with benzodiazepines or other CNS depressants, including alcohol, may result in profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, and death.

sections.pathophysiology.3.quote: When people take high doses of opioids, it can lead to an overdose, with the slowing or stopping of breathing and sometimes death.

sections.risk_factors.1.quote: Concomitant use of opioids with benzodiazepines or other CNS depressants, including alcohol, may result in profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, and death.

sections.signs_symptoms.0.quote: Opioid intoxication is classically described as a triad of symptoms consisting of reduced consciousness, slow and/or shallow breathing, and miosis (i.e., pinpoint pupils).

sections.signs_symptoms.2.quote: Concomitant use of opioids with benzodiazepines or other CNS depressants, including alcohol, may result in profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, and death.

sections.signs_symptoms.4.quote: The most common are gastrointestinal effects, including nausea, vomiting, and constipation.

sections.diagnostics.3.quote: The presence of opioids in a client is not routinely measured in the blood but rather is detected using urine drug screens.

sections.complications.0.quote: Concomitant use of opioids with benzodiazepines or other CNS depressants, including alcohol, may result in profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, and death.

sections.nursing_care.2.quote: These signs constitute a medical emergency and necessitate the use of an opioid antagonist such as naloxone hydrochloride (discussed in the following section) along with the response of emergency medical services.

sections.nursing_care.3.quote: Assess for changes in level of consciousness and respirations.

sections.patient_teaching.0.quote: Share opioids with family or friends because this practice can lead to harm or even death.

sections.patient_teaching.1.quote: Store your medicine safely where children or pets can't reach it.

sections.patient_teaching.2.quote: Opioid intoxication is classically described as a triad of symptoms consisting of reduced consciousness, slow and/or shallow breathing, and miosis (i.e., pinpoint pupils).

sections.patient_teaching.3.quote: If you think someone is having an opioid overdose: Call 911 immediately .

sections.patient_teaching.4.quote: Naloxone hydrochloride should be coprescribed to clients who are at greater risk for opioid overdose.
